analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act and replaces it with a tax credit for buying private insurance.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had no cosponsors, never received a hearing or a vote and died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the Affordable Care Act and every related provision of the 2010 health law, returning federal law to what existed before 2010. In its place, it would create a refundable income tax credit — up to $1,000 per adult per year plus half of any premium above that — for people who buy private health insurance on their own, with the government allowed to pay insurers directly in advance. It would not restore any requirement that insurers sell coverage to people with pre-existing conditions.
analysis.who_benefits: The bill's direct benefit goes to individuals who buy their own private coverage, who could claim a credit of $1,000 per adult plus half of premium costs above that, phasing out above $65,000 of income for singles and $105,000 for couples [S3]. It also helps health insurers by removing the ACA's rules on what they must cover, who they must sell to, and how they must spend premium dollars, while routing new federal payments directly to them [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Self-purchased private insurance buyers and insurers

how_it_helps.text: Creates a refundable tax credit for health insurance costs — $1,000 per year for the taxpayer, $1,000 for a spouse, and $500 per child, plus 50% of any premium above those base amounts — available even to people who owe no income tax [S3].

The credit shrinks as income rises, phasing out over a $10,000 range above $65,000 for single filers and $105,000 for joint filers, so it targets middle- and lower-income buyers of individual coverage [S3].
Lets the Treasury send credit payments directly to a person's insurance company in advance during the year, so people do not have to front the full premium and wait for a refund [S2][S3].
Excludes months when someone is covered by an employer plan, Medicare, Medicaid, or CHIP, so the credit is aimed only at the individual insurance market [S3].

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the people who would bear the cost are those who relied on ACA protections and subsidies: people with pre-existing conditions, who under restored pre-2010 law could again be denied coverage or charged unaffordable prices; and lower-income households who would receive a credit far smaller than the ACA's subsidies or Medicaid expansion. The repeal also strips consumer protections such as bans on lifetime coverage limits. The federal treasury pays for the credit, and the lost ACA-related revenue and spending are repealed with it.
analysis.who_pays_short: People with pre-existing conditions and ACA subsidy recipients

drawbacks.text: Repealing the ACA restores the pre-2010 legal landscape, under which insurers could deny coverage or charge more for pre-existing conditions, impose lifetime limits, and exclude required benefits — the bill sets no requirement that insurers cover sick applicants at any price [S2][S3].

The credit is much smaller than the ACA's subsidies for many households and is unavailable to anyone covered by an employer plan, Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, VA, or military coverage, so it does not replace the coverage pathways the ACA created [S3].

A flat credit of this size buys little of an actual family premium, and the bill leaves the individual insurance market without the ACA's rules on benefit standards or medical loss ratios, so the money flows to insurers without a guarantee of adequate coverage [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The credit would genuinely help a narrow group — mostly healthier, middle-income people buying individual coverage — but the bill pairs it with a full repeal of the ACA, including guaranteed issue, subsidy levels, and Medicaid expansion, without any replacement mechanism for people those provisions covered. The protection lost is worth far more to the people who depend on it than the credit gained. As a designed policy, it substitutes a modest tax credit for a broad coverage and consumer-protection framework.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to eight House committees, some of which referred pieces to subcommittees, and no committee or subcommittee ever acted on it, so it expired at the end of the 112th Congress in January 2013.

narrative.text: Kay Granger introduced the bill in the House on February 10, 2011, and it was referred to eight committees: Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and the Workforce, House Administration, Appropriations, Natural Resources, Judiciary, and Rules [S1][S5].
Subcommittees received referrals — Indian and Alaska Native Affairs, Health, and Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions — but no markup, hearing, or floor action followed [S5].
No member signed on as a cosponsor, and the bill never received a vote in either chamber before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the ACA's protections remained in place: people with pre-existing conditions, young adults on their parents' plans, and households receiving ACA subsidies or Medicaid expansion kept their coverage pathways. Health insurers also kept operating under the ACA's rules rather than the deregulated pre-2010 rules this bill would have restored.

for.name: Rep. Kay Granger
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and secured its referral to eight House committees.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill without scheduling any markup or hearing; its Health Subcommittee received the referral in February 2011 and took no further action.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral for the tax credit provisions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action on it during the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Only one member — a Texas Republican — sponsored the bill, no cosponsors signed on, and no vote was ever recorded, so the partisan shape was never tested.

industries.note: The bill removes the ACA's requirements that insurers cover people with pre-existing conditions, meet benefit standards, and spend a share of premiums on medical care, while still routing federal credit payments directly to insurers. Insurers would collect federal money without any guarantee that sick customers can buy coverage.

Healthy buyers of individual coverage would gain a refundable credit of up to $1,000 per adult plus half of premium excess, paid in advance. Buyers with health problems would lose the ACA's guaranteed-issue and rating protections, so the same provision cuts in opposite directions by health status.
